proofs.proof_tex:
Let \(\mathscr E=\sigma(E_0)\).  By the definition of \(z_0\),
\(z_0=\mathbb E_P[Z_j\mid E_0]\) is \(\mathscr E\)-measurable.  Consequently,
adjoining \(z_0\) to the conditioning field generated by \(E_0\) does not
change any conditional expectation below.  By \texttt{def:target} and
linearity of conditional expectation,
\[
\tau_n(z_0)=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\pi_s\left\{
\frac1{n_s}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}\mathbb E_P[B_{si}(1)\mid z_0,E_0]
-\frac1{n_s}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}\mathbb E_P[B_{si}(0)\mid z_0,E_0]
\right\}.
\tag{1}
\]
Assumption \texttt{ass:consistency} and the definition of
\(\bar B_s^{\mathrm{obs}}\) give
\[
\frac1{n_s}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}\mathbb E_P[B_{si}(1)\mid z_0,E_0]
=\mathbb E_P[\bar B_s^{\mathrm{obs}}\mid z_0,E_0].
\tag{2}
\]
Assumption \texttt{ass:event-transport} gives, for each cohort,
\[
\frac1{n_s}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}\mathbb E_P[B_{si}(0)\mid z_0,E_0]
=m_s(z_{0s}).
\tag{3}
\]
Substitution of (2)--(3) into (1) proves
\[
\tau_n(z_0)=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\pi_s
\{\mathbb E_P[\bar B_s^{\mathrm{obs}}\mid z_0,E_0]-m_s(z_{0s})\}.
\]
Assumption \texttt{ass:historical-regression} separately identifies
\(m_s(x)\) as the observed-law conditional mean of an untreated
pseudo-event response at \(X_{st}=x\).  Thus consistency and event transport
prove the equality between the causal contrast and the observed-law
functional; that equality is not introduced as a definition of the causal
target.

Fix a successful cohort \(s\), abbreviate
\(\bar B_s^{\mathrm{obs}}\) by \(\bar B_s\), and hold
\(\gamma\in\mathbb R^{q_r}\) fixed.  The event part of the criterion in
\texttt{def:fwl-regression} satisfies the exact identity
\[
\frac1{n_s}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}
(B_{si}^{\mathrm{obs}}-\theta-e_0^\top\gamma)^2
=\frac1{n_s}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}(B_{si}^{\mathrm{obs}}-\bar B_s)^2
+(\bar B_s-\theta-e_0^\top\gamma)^2.
\tag{4}
\]
Consequently, for fixed \(\gamma\), the unique minimizing event coefficient is
\[
\theta=\bar B_s^{\mathrm{obs}}-e_0^\top\gamma.
\tag{5}
\]
At (5), the event criterion is independent of \(\gamma\).  Up to the first,
constant term in (4), the profiled criterion is therefore
\[
\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}
w_{st}\{Q_{sti}-b_r(u_{st})^\top\gamma\}^2,
\tag{6}
\]
which is exactly the historical weighted least-squares problem in
\texttt{def:feasible-estimator}.  Passage of the normalized-shape test implies
\(L_s>0\) and
\[
G_s\succeq c_GL_sI_{q_r}\succ0.
\]
Hence (6) has the unique minimizer \(\widehat\gamma_s\), and profiling gives
\[
\widehat\theta_s
=\bar B_s^{\mathrm{obs}}-e_0^\top\widehat\gamma_s.
\tag{7}
\]
Using the definitions of \(\widehat m_s\), \(\theta_{\mathrm{FWL}}\), and
\(\widehat\tau\), on every sample for which all selected fits exist,
\[
\theta_{\mathrm{FWL}}
=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\pi_s
(\bar B_s^{\mathrm{obs}}-e_0^\top\widehat\gamma_s)
=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\pi_s(\bar B_s^{\mathrm{obs}}-\widehat m_s)
=\widehat\tau.
\]

Under the first specialization, \(S=1\) and \(\sum_s\pi_s=1\) imply
\(\pi_1=1\).  The identifying equality in
\texttt{lem:identification-fwl} and the restriction
\(m_1(x)=x+\Delta_0\) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\tau_n(z_0)
&=\mathbb E_P[\bar B_1^{\mathrm{obs}}\mid z_0,E_0]-m_1(z_{01})\\
&=\mathbb E_P[\bar B_1^{\mathrm{obs}}\mid z_0,E_0]-z_{01}-\Delta_0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]
When the scalar proxy is the event cohort's baseline outcome, \(z_{01}\) is
its conditional baseline mean.  When \(\Delta_0\) is the untreated
cohort-average post-minus-baseline mean change, (8) is treated post minus
treated baseline minus the untreated post-minus-baseline change.  This is the
canonical conditional finite-cohort two-period difference-in-differences
contrast.

For the second specialization define the cohort effect
\[
\tau_s=\frac1{n_s}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}
\mathbb E_P[B_{si}(1)-B_{si}(0)\mid z_0,E_0].
\]
Homogeneity across cohorts means that \(\tau_s=\tau^{\mathrm{com}}\) for every
\(s\).  By \texttt{def:target} and \(\sum_s\pi_s=1\),
\[
\tau_n(z_0)=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\pi_s\tau_s
=\tau^{\mathrm{com}}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\pi_s
=\tau^{\mathrm{com}}.
\tag{9}
\]
The stipulated absence of carry-over beyond \(h=0\) makes this common
terminal-level contrast the contemporaneous finite-cohort treatment effect on
the level-wealth path in \texttt{def:buyhold-level}.  This causal
interpretation uses the stated specialization; it does not follow from the
aggregation identity alone.

Put \(D=Sd\).  For any class member define, only for this proof,
\[
Y=\Sigma^{-1/2}(Z_1-z_0).
\]
The definitions of \(z_0\) and \(\Sigma\), together with positive
definiteness from \texttt{ass:donor-ellipticity}, imply
\(\mathbb E_P[YY^\top\mid E_0]=I_D\).  Taking traces, applying conditional
Jensen's inequality to the nonnegative random variable \(\lVert Y\rVert_2^2\),
and using \texttt{ass:donor-fourth-moment} give
\[
D^2
=\{\mathbb E_P[\lVert Y\rVert_2^2\mid E_0]\}^2
\le \mathbb E_P[\lVert Y\rVert_2^4\mid E_0]
\le B.
\tag{10}
\]
Thus \(B<D^2\) gives an empty class.  Fix henceforth \(B\ge D^2\), an
admissible interior query, and one cohort \(s_*\) having fixed positive
weight; hold all other cohorts fixed across the two laws.

For sufficiently small fixed constants \(c_p,c_L>0\), set
\[
L_T=\lfloor c_L\log(T\vee2)\rfloor\vee1,
\qquad
p_T=c_p\frac{L_T}{T},
\]
where \(c_L\lvert\log\rho_0\rvert<1\).  Since
\(p_T\asymp \log(T)/T\), whereas
\(\rho_0^{L_T}\asymp T^{-c_L\lvert\log\rho_0\rvert}\), decreasing
\(c_p\), if necessary, gives
\[
2p_T\le \beta_0\rho_0^{L_T-1}
\tag{11}
\]
for all sufficiently large \(T\).  Let \(A_T\) be a Euclidean ball centered
at \(z_{0s_*}\), contained in \([0,1]^d\), and having Lebesgue measure
\(p_T\).  The interior-path condition permits this choice for large \(T\),
and its radius satisfies
\[
h_T\asymp p_T^{1/d}
\asymp\left\{\frac{\log(T\vee2)}{T}\right\}^{1/d}.
\tag{12}
\]

Partition the calendar into deterministic consecutive blocks of length
\(L_T\), apart from a final shorter block.  Independently across blocks draw
\(G_b\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_T)\).  Conditional on \(G_b=1\), draw the
selected cohort's design points in block \(b\) independently and uniformly on
\(A_T\); conditional on \(G_b=0\), draw them independently and uniformly on
\([0,1]^d\setminus A_T\).  At each time the marginal density is
\[
p_T\frac{\mathbf 1_{A_T}(x)}{p_T}
+(1-p_T)\frac{\mathbf 1_{A_T^c}(x)}{1-p_T}=1.
\tag{13}
\]
The other cohorts may have independent uniform designs.  Hence
\texttt{ass:design-density} holds because \(c_X\le1\le C_X\).  At lags at
least \(L_T\), the two relevant sigma-fields involve independent block
variables.  At a smaller lag, only the block crossing the separating cut can
be shared.  Conditional on that shared Bernoulli variable, the two sides are
independent; expanding the two-component mixture bounds its
absolute-regularity distance from the product law by
\(2p_T(1-p_T)\le2p_T\).  Since
\(\rho_0^\ell\ge\rho_0^{L_T-1}\) for \(1\le\ell<L_T\), (11) implies
\[
\beta_P(\ell_{\mathrm{mix}}\mid E_0)
\le
\begin{cases}
2p_T,&1\le\ell_{\mathrm{mix}}<L_T,\\
0,&\ell_{\mathrm{mix}}\ge L_T,
\end{cases}
\le\beta_0\rho_0^{\ell_{\mathrm{mix}}}.
\tag{14}
\]

Choose a bounded H\"older carrier \(g\) lying in the interior of the response
range.  Give its weighted cohort surface a nonzero affine component at
\(z_0\) when \(\lambda>1\), and an asymmetric \(\lambda\)-cusp there when
\(0<\lambda\le1\); fixed scaling places the carrier inside the H\"older and
two-sided-modulus envelopes.  Let \(\psi\) be a fixed smooth bump supported on
the unit ball with \(\psi(0)=1\), and define in cohort \(s_*\)
\[
m_0(x)=g(x),
\qquad
m_1(x)=g(x)+c_bh_T^\lambda
\psi\left(\frac{x-z_{0s_*}}{h_T}\right).
\tag{15}
\]
Take \(c_b>0\) small enough that both surfaces remain in
\(\mathcal H_d(\lambda,L)\) and in the response interior.  When
\(\lambda>1\), the bump increment over a displacement of norm \(\delta\) is
at most \(Cc_bh_T^{\lambda-1}\delta\) for \(\delta\le h_T\), and at most
\(Cc_bh_T^\lambda\le Cc_bh_T^{\lambda-1}\delta\) for \(\delta>h_T\).
It therefore cannot cancel the fixed affine lower modulus.  When
\(0<\lambda\le1\), the increment is at most \(Cc_b\delta^\lambda\), so it
cannot cancel the carrier's cusp lower modulus when \(c_b\) is small.  The
H\"older upper inequality and the covariance eigenvalue bounds give the upper
standardized modulus.  Thus both laws obey
\texttt{ass:local-two-sided-modulus} with
\(\kappa=\min\{\lambda,1\}\).

Conditional on the complete design
\(\mathscr X=\sigma\{X_{st}:s\le S,t\le T\}\), draw bounded historical
response paths independently across units from kernels having mean
\(m_\ell(X_{st})\); these kernels may vary by unit.  Draw bounded event
outcomes independently of \(\mathscr X\) with a common mean under the two
laws, and complete untreated event potential outcomes so that their
cohort-average conditional means are \(m_\ell(z_{0s})\).  Then
\[
\mathbb E[B_{si}^{\mathrm{obs}}\mid\mathscr X,E_0]
=\mathbb E[B_{si}^{\mathrm{obs}}\mid E_0],
\qquad
\mathbb E[\varepsilon_{sti}\mid\mathscr X,E_0]=0.
\tag{16}
\]
For the donors use, under both laws, independent copies of
\[
Z_j=z_0+U_j,
\qquad
U_j\sim\operatorname{Unif}\{\pm\sqrt D\,e_k:1\le k\le D\},
\]
independently of the panel.  Symmetry gives
\[
\mathbb E[U_j\mid E_0]=0,
\qquad
\mathbb E[U_jU_j^\top\mid E_0]=I_D,
\qquad
\mathbb E[\lVert U_j\rVert_2^4\mid E_0]=D^2\le B.
\tag{17}
\]
Thus \(\Sigma=I_D\), including at \(B=D^2\), and the donor data carry no
information distinguishing the two laws.  Take
\(X_{st}^{\mathrm{obs}}=X_{st}\).  Set observed and historical potential
outcomes according to consistency, make historical potential outcomes
invariant to event treatment, and make every potential outcome invariant to
other units' assignments.  Choose all random wealth values in a compact
subinterval of \((0,B)\), so that the primitive buy-and-hold representation
can be realized with a positive common initial wealth and returns strictly
greater than \(-1\).  Equations (13)--(17) and these completions verify every
member property of
\(\mathcal M_{N,T,\mathbf n}^{\dagger}(\lambda)\), including support, exact
coordinates, limited anticipation, no spillovers, event transport, and both
full-design centering restrictions.

Let \(\mathcal A_T\) be the event that no calendar block is active.  Since the
number of blocks is \(T/L_T+O(1)\),
\[
P(\mathcal A_T\mid E_0)
=(1-p_T)^{T/L_T+O(1)}\longrightarrow e^{-c_p}>0.
\tag{18}
\]
On \(\mathcal A_T\), every selected-cohort design point lies outside \(A_T\),
where the surfaces in (15) agree.  All remaining observed kernels are common,
so the complete observed-data laws coincide on this event.  Therefore
\[
\int\min\{dP_{0,T},dP_{1,T}\}
\ge P(\mathcal A_T\mid E_0)\ge c>0.
\tag{19}
\]
The observed event mean is common, whereas event transport changes the
selected cohort's untreated event mean by \(c_bh_T^\lambda\).  The
identification equality in \texttt{lem:identification-fwl}, the fixed positive
weight \(\pi_{s_*}\), and (12) give
\[
\lvert\tau_{n,P_{1,T}}(z_0)-\tau_{n,P_{0,T}}(z_0)\rvert
\ge ch_T^\lambda
\asymp\left\{\frac{\log(T\vee2)}{T}\right\}^{\lambda/d}.
\tag{20}
\]
For the finitely many \(T\) preceding (11), use a fixed interior ball and two
sufficiently close bounded response kernels with positive affinity and fixed
nonzero target separation; decreasing the common constant makes (19)--(20)
valid for every positive \(T\).

Write the two target values as \(\tau_0,\tau_1\) and their separation as
\(\Delta=\lvert\tau_1-\tau_0\rvert\).  For any estimator
\(\widehat\tau\), the triangle inequality gives
\[
\mathbf 1\{\lvert\widehat\tau-\tau_0\rvert\ge\Delta/2\}
+\mathbf 1\{\lvert\widehat\tau-\tau_1\rvert\ge\Delta/2\}\ge1.
\]
Integrating this inequality against the overlap measure in (19) yields
\[
\max_{\ell\in\{0,1\}}
\mathbb E_{P_{\ell,T}}
[\{\widehat\tau-\tau_\ell\}^2\mid E_0]
\ge \frac{\Delta^2}{8}\int\min\{dP_{0,T},dP_{1,T}\}
\ge cR_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}.
\tag{21}
\]
This holds for every estimator, so it gives the stated conditional minimax
mean squared error lower bound.

Finally, decrease \(c_p\), if needed, so that the affinity in (19) is larger
than \(2\alpha+a_0\) for some \(a_0>0\).  If \(C\) is a uniformly
conditionally \((1-\alpha)\)-honest interval, then
\[
\int \mathbf 1\{\tau_0\in C,\ \tau_1\in C\}
\min\{dP_{0,T},dP_{1,T}\}
\ge \int\min\{dP_{0,T},dP_{1,T}\}-2\alpha
\ge a_0.
\]
On the integrand's event, \(\operatorname{length}(C)\ge\Delta\).  Hence its
worst-case conditional expected length is at least
\(a_0\Delta\ge c_\alpha R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}^{1/2}\).  The chosen event
path lies in \(\mathcal Z_+\), so its conditional query probability is one
and hence at least \(c_X\).  This proves the lemma for every compatible
envelope without an anti-clustering premise.

Put
\[
a:=\frac{2\lambda}{2\lambda+d}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
q:=\frac{2\lambda}{d}.
\]
The declared restrictions \(\lambda>0\) and \(d>0\) imply \(a\in(0,1)\) and \(q>0\).  We first establish the weighted arithmetic--geometric mean inequality used below.  For \(u>0\), define
\[
\phi(u):=au+(1-a)-u^a.
\]
Then \(\phi(1)=0\), while
\[
\phi'(u)=a\bigl(1-u^{a-1}\bigr).
\]
Because \(a-1<0\), this derivative is negative for \(0<u<1\), vanishes at \(u=1\), and is positive for \(u>1\).  Thus \(u=1\) is a global minimizer and \(\phi(u)\geq0\).  Substituting \(u=x/y\) and multiplying by \(y>0\) proves
\[
x^a y^{1-a}\leq ax+(1-a)y,
\qquad x>0,quad y>0.
\tag{1}
\]
The definitions of \(a\) and \(q\) give
\[
q(1-a)
=\frac{2\lambda}{d}\frac{d}{2\lambda+d}
=\frac{2\lambda}{2\lambda+d}
=a.
\tag{2}
\]
For every cohort \(s\), positivity of the integers \(T\) and \(n_s\) permits applying (1) with \(x=n_s^{-1}\) and \(y=T^{-q}\).  Using (2),
\[
\begin{aligned}
(Tn_s)^{-2\lambda/(2\lambda+d)}
&=n_s^{-a}T^{-a}\\
&=(n_s^{-1})^a(T^{-q})^{1-a}\\
&\leq a n_s^{-1}+(1-a)T^{-q}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
\]
The declared cohort weights satisfy \(\pi_s>0\) and \(\sum_{s=1}^S\pi_s=1\).  Hence
\[
\sum_{s=1}^S\pi_s^2
\leq\left(\sum_{s=1}^S\pi_s\right)^2
=1.
\tag{4}
\]
Multiplying (3) by \(\pi_s^2\), summing over \(s\), applying (4), and invoking the definitions of \(R_{\mathrm{sm}}\) and \(R_{\mathrm{tr}}\) in \(\texttt{def:rate-frontier}\), we obtain
\[
R_{\mathrm{sm}}
\leq aR_{\mathrm{tr}}+(1-a)T^{-q}.
\tag{5}
\]

For every positive integer \(T\), one has \(\log(T\vee2)\geq\log2>0\).  Therefore, because \(q>0\), the definition of \(R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}\) in \(\texttt{def:rate-frontier}\) yields
\[
T^{-q}
\leq(\log2)^{-q}
\left\{\frac{\log(T\vee2)}{T}\right\}^{q}
=(\log2)^{-q}R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}.
\tag{6}
\]
Combining (5) and (6), and using \(cx+ey\leq(c+e)(x\vee y)\) for nonnegative \(c,e,x,y\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
R_{\mathrm{sm}}
&\leq aR_{\mathrm{tr}}+(1-a)(\log2)^{-q}R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}\\
&\leq\bigl\{a+(1-a)(\log2)^{-q}\bigr\}
\bigl(R_{\mathrm{tr}}\vee R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}\bigr)\\
&=C_{\lambda,d}
\bigl(R_{\mathrm{tr}}\vee R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}\bigr),
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}
\]
where the last equality follows from \(1-a=d/(2\lambda+d)\) and \(q=2\lambda/d\).  Since \(0<\log2<1\) and \(q>0\),
\[
C_{\lambda,d}=a+(1-a)(\log2)^{-q}
\geq a+(1-a)=1.
\tag{8}
\]
Define \(A:=R_{\mathrm{tr}}\vee R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}\) and \(G:=A\vee R_{\mathrm{don}}\).  Every rate component is positive by \(\texttt{def:rate-frontier}\).  Its definition of \(R_{\star,\beta}\), together with (7)--(8), gives
\[
G
\leq R_{\star,\beta}
=G\vee R_{\mathrm{sm}}
\leq G\vee(C_{\lambda,d}A)
\leq C_{\lambda,d}G.
\tag{9}
\]
Consequently,
\[
R_{\star,\beta}
\asymp_{\lambda,d}
R_{\mathrm{tr}}\vee R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}\vee R_{\mathrm{don}},
\]
with comparison constants \(1\) and \(C_{\lambda,d}\), uniformly in \(N,T,S\) and all positive replication counts.

Suppose next that \(T\geq3\).  Then \(T\vee2=T\) and \(\log T\geq\log3>1\), so
\[
T^{-q}
\leq\left(\frac{\log T}{T}\right)^q
=R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}.
\tag{10}
\]
Substitution of (10) into (5), followed by \(a\in(0,1)\), proves
\[
R_{\mathrm{sm}}
\leq aR_{\mathrm{tr}}+(1-a)R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}
\leq R_{\mathrm{tr}}\vee R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}.
\tag{11}
\]
Taking the maximum with the remaining components in \(\texttt{def:rate-frontier}\) therefore gives
\[
R_{\star,\beta}
=R_{\mathrm{tr}}\vee R_{\mathrm{sp},\beta}\vee R_{\mathrm{don}}.
\tag{12}
\]

By \(\texttt{def:rate-frontier}\), \(R_{\mathrm{don}}=N^{-\kappa}\).  Along any joint growth array, this channel is negligible relative to \(A\) precisely when
\[
N^{-\kappa}=o(A),
\]
and it dominates \(A\) precisely when
\[
A=o(N^{-\kappa}).
\]
Because \(\kappa>0\) and \(A>0\), the boundary relation \(N^{-\kappa}\asymp A\) is equivalent, after applying the decreasing map \(x\mapsto x^{-1/\kappa}\) and absorbing fixed comparison constants, to
\[
N\asymp A^{-1/\kappa}.
\]
These comparisons have the asserted oracle/generated-center interpretation whenever a separate statistical result establishes \(R_{\star,\beta}\) as the sharp risk of the experiment; equations (1)--(12) do not assert that statistical premise.

For the independent-calendar class, or under the separately imposed fixed-query local-small-ball or anti-clustering condition specified in \(\texttt{def:rate-frontier}\), the delivered spacing component is
\[
R_{\mathrm{sp}}=T^{-q}.
\]
Equation (5) consequently implies
\[
R_{\mathrm{sm}}
\leq aR_{\mathrm{tr}}+(1-a)R_{\mathrm{sp}}
\leq R_{\mathrm{tr}}\vee R_{\mathrm{sp}}.
\tag{13}
\]
The corresponding definition of \(R_\star\) in \(\texttt{def:rate-frontier}\) and (13) then give the exact identity
\[
R_\star
=R_{\mathrm{tr}}\vee R_{\mathrm{sm}}\vee R_{\mathrm{sp}}\vee R_{\mathrm{don}}
=R_{\mathrm{tr}}\vee R_{\mathrm{sp}}\vee R_{\mathrm{don}}.
\]

Finally, \(\texttt{ass:exact-training-coordinates}\) states \(X_{st}^{\mathrm{obs}}=X_{st}\).  Thus the historical regression coordinate is observed exactly, so there is no measurement-error convolution to invert.  Consistently, the exhaustive maxima defining \(R_{\star,\beta}\) and \(R_\star\) in \(\texttt{def:rate-frontier}\) contain neither a deconvolution component nor a separate moving-Gram component.  The same definition uses \(\kappa=\min\{\lambda,1\}\).  If \(\lambda>1\), then \(\kappa=1\), and hence
\[
R_{\mathrm{don}}=N^{-\kappa}=N^{-1}.
\]
This proves every asserted algebraic conclusion and preserves the theorem's stated distinction between those conclusions and statistical sharpness.

It suffices to construct one admissible triangular array.  Fix
\[
H=0,\qquad p=S=d=1,\qquad \lambda=\kappa=1,
\qquad \pi_1=1,
\]
where the last equality follows from the normalization of the single cohort
weight.  Choose
\[
B=16,\qquad c_X=C_X=c_\Sigma=C_\Sigma=1,
\qquad \delta_0=\frac14,\qquad
c_{\mathrm{mod}}=C_{\mathrm{mod}}=1.
\]
Then \(D=Sd=1\), so in particular \(B>D^2\) and the donor-envelope
compatibility condition is satisfied.  Choose any fixed \(\beta_0>0\) and
\(\rho_0\in(0,1)\).  Take \(L\) at least the finite
\(\mathcal H_1(1,\cdot)\)-norm of the affine function introduced below, use
the uniform order-zero kernel
\[
K(u)={\bf 1}\{|u|\leq1\},
\]
and choose the normalized-shape threshold so that \(0<c_G\leq1\).  This
kernel is nonnegative, bounded, compactly supported, and equal to one in a
neighborhood of zero, as required in the definition of \(K\).  Since
\(\lambda=1\), the definitions of \(r\), \(b_r\), and \(e_0\) give
\[
r=\lceil1\rceil-1=0,\qquad b_0(u)=e_0=1.
\]
Let \(E_0\) be constant, set \(z_0=1/2\) and
\(\mathcal Z_+=\{1/2\}\), and, for each positive integer \(T\), put
\[
n_1=N=T^2.
\]

We first construct the historical sample.  Write \(X_t=X_{1t}\), and let
\(X_1,\ldots,X_T\) be independent and uniformly distributed on
\([0,1]\).  Define
\[
m(x)=8+x-\frac12,
\qquad
Q_{1ti}=m(X_t)+\frac12U_{ti},
\]
where the variables \((U_{ti})_{t,i}\) are mutually independent Rademacher
variables and are independent of the complete design.  Because
\(m([0,1])=[15/2,17/2]\),
\[
7\leq Q_{1ti}\leq9\leq B,
\qquad
\mathbb E_P[Q_{1ti}\mid X_t=x,E_0]=m(x).
\]
Thus \texttt{ass:bounded-historical-wealth} and
\texttt{ass:historical-regression} hold.  The affine function \(m\) belongs
to \(\mathcal H_1(1,L)\) by the choice of \(L\), which verifies
\texttt{ass:holder-smoothness}.  The conditional density of every \(X_t\)
is one on \([0,1]\), so \texttt{ass:design-density} holds for the displayed
values of \(c_X\) and \(C_X\).  Independence over calendar time implies
\[
\beta_P(\ell_{\mathrm{mix}}\mid E_0)=0
\leq\beta_0\rho_0^{\ell_{\mathrm{mix}}}
\qquad(\ell_{\mathrm{mix}}\geq1),
\]
which verifies \texttt{ass:temporal-mixing}.  Finally set
\(X_{1t}^{\mathrm{obs}}=X_t\), as required by
\texttt{ass:exact-training-coordinates}.

Independently of the historical sample, let
\[
Z_j=\frac12+V_j,
\]
where \(V_1,\ldots,V_N\) are independent Rademacher variables.  Then
\[
\mathbb E_P[Z_j\mid E_0]=z_0,
\qquad
\Sigma=\operatorname{Var}_P(Z_j\mid E_0)=1,
\]
and
\[
\mathbb E_P\!\left[
 \left|\Sigma^{-1/2}(Z_j-z_0)\right|^4\,\middle|\,E_0
\right]=1\leq B.
\]
These equalities verify the defining relation for \(z_0\),
\texttt{ass:donor-ellipticity}, and \texttt{ass:donor-fourth-moment}; the
construction also verifies \texttt{ass:donor-replication} and, by the stated
independence, \texttt{ass:donor-independence}.  If
\(0<\delta\leq\delta_0\), then every \(z_0+u\) with \(|u|\leq\delta\)
lies in \([0,1]\).  Since \(\Sigma=1\), \texttt{def:local-modulus} gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\omega_P(\delta;z_0)
&=\sup_{|u|\leq\delta}|m(z_0+u)-m(z_0)|\\
&=\sup_{|u|\leq\delta}|u|=\delta.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence \texttt{ass:local-two-sided-modulus} holds with the displayed modulus
constants.  Moreover,
\[
\operatorname{dist}(z_0,\partial[0,1])=\frac12\geq\delta_0,
\qquad
P\{z_0\in\mathcal Z_+\}=1\geq c_X,
\]
which verifies \texttt{ass:interior-event-path} and
\texttt{ass:positive-query-region}.

We next specify the causal variables.  Define the design-measurable event
shock
\[
\Gamma={\bf 1}\{X_1\leq1/4\}
\]
and, for every \(i\), set
\[
B_{1i}(0)=8,\qquad B_{1i}(1)=8+\Gamma,
\qquad B_{1i}^{\mathrm{obs}}=B_{1i}(1).
\]
Define \(B_{1i}(a,\mathbf a_{-1i})=B_{1i}(a)\) for every other-unit
assignment vector, and define \(Q_{1ti}(a)=Q_{1ti}\) for both
\(a\in\{0,1\}\).  These definitions verify, respectively,
\texttt{ass:consistency}, \texttt{ass:historical-consistency},
\texttt{ass:no-spillovers}, and \texttt{ass:limited-anticipation}.  They
also yield \(0\leq B_{1i}(a)\leq9<B\), so
\texttt{ass:bounded-event-wealth} holds.  The construction is compatible
with \texttt{def:buyhold-level}: take
\[
W_{1i,-1}=1,
\qquad
R_{1i0}(a)=B_{1i}(a)-1>-1;
\]
then \(W_{1i,-1}\{1+R_{1i0}(a)\}=B_{1i}(a)\), as required when \(H=0\).
Since \(m(z_0)=8\),
\[
\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}
\mathbb E_P[B_{1i}(0)\mid z_0,E_0]
=8=m(z_0),
\]
which is exactly \texttt{ass:event-transport}.  Conditional on the complete
design and \(E_0\), every event outcome is constant, while the historical
path of unit \(i\) is a measurable function of
\((U_{ti})_{t=1}^T\).  Independence of these vectors across \(i\) therefore
gives \texttt{ass:cross-unit-independence}.  Together with the preceding
checks, every member property in \texttt{def:panel-law-class} is satisfied;
hence the resulting law \(P_T\) belongs to
\(\mathcal M_{N,T,\mathbf n}(1)\).

The causal target is distinct from the realized event mean.  Because
\(z_0\) and \(E_0\) are constant and \(P(\Gamma=1)=1/4\),
\texttt{def:target} gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\tau_n(z_0)
&=\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}
  \mathbb E_P[B_{1i}(1)-B_{1i}(0)\mid z_0,E_0]\\
&=\mathbb E_P[\Gamma]=\frac14,
\end{aligned}
\qquad
\bar B_1^{\mathrm{obs}}=8+\Gamma.
\]

We now analyze \texttt{def:feasible-estimator}.  Its generated and projected
centers are
\[
\bar Z=\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N Z_j,
\qquad
\widetilde z=\Pi_{[0,1]}(\bar Z).
\]
Metric projection onto \([0,1]\) fixes \(z_0\) and cannot increase distance
from \(z_0\).  Therefore, by the independence and first two moments of the
Rademacher variables,
\[
|\widetilde z-z_0|
\leq\left|\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^NV_j\right|,
\qquad
\mathbb E_P[(\widetilde z-z_0)^2\mid E_0]
\leq\frac1N=T^{-2}.
\]
For all sufficiently large \(T\), the truncation by one in the initial
bandwidth is inactive and, since \(n_1=N=T^2\), that bandwidth equals
\[
\underline h_T
=C_h\left[(Tn_1)^{-1/3}
\vee\frac{\log(T\vee2)}T\vee N^{-1/2}\right]
=C_h\frac{\log T}{T}.
\]
Define
\[
I_T=\{t:|X_t-\widetilde z|\leq\underline h_T\},
\qquad
\mathcal A_T=\{|I_T|>0\}.
\]
For every fixed \(\widetilde z\in[0,1]\), the Lebesgue measure of
\([\widetilde z-\underline h_T,\widetilde z+\underline h_T]\cap[0,1]\)
is at least \(\underline h_T\).  Donor independence and the independent
uniform design therefore imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(\mathcal A_T^c\mid E_0,\widetilde z)
&\leq(1-\underline h_T)^T\\
&\leq\exp(-T\underline h_T)=T^{-C_h}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently \(P(\mathcal A_T^c\mid E_0)\to0\).

On \(\mathcal A_T\), the local mass and order-zero Gram matrix at the first
candidate satisfy
\[
L_1=n_1|I_T|,\qquad G_1=n_1|I_T|,
\qquad \lambda_{\min}(G_1/L_1)=1\geq c_G.
\]
Thus the selector accepts the initial candidate, and its least-squares
intercept is
\[
\widehat m_1
=\frac1{n_1|I_T|}
  \sum_{t\in I_T}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}Q_{1ti}.
\]
Its conditional-mean component differs from \(m(z_0)=8\) by at most
\[
\frac1{|I_T|}\sum_{t\in I_T}|m(X_t)-m(z_0)|
\leq\underline h_T+|\widetilde z-z_0|.
\]
Conditional on the design and donors, the Rademacher component has mean zero
and variance
\[
\operatorname{Var}_P\!\left(
\frac1{2n_1|I_T|}\sum_{t\in I_T}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}U_{ti}
\,\middle|\,(X_t)_{t=1}^T,(Z_j)_{j=1}^N,E_0
\right)
=\frac1{4n_1|I_T|}\leq\frac1{4n_1}.
\]
At every successful order-zero candidate the fitted intercept is an average
of observations in \([7,9]\); if all candidates fail, its defined value is
zero.  Hence \((\widehat m_1-8)^2\leq64\) on
\(\mathcal A_T^c\).  Splitting according to \(\mathcal A_T\), and using
the preceding conditional bias and variance bounds, gives a fixed finite
constant \(C\) such that
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_P[(\widehat m_1-8)^2\mid E_0]
&\leq C\left\{
\underline h_T^2+N^{-1}+n_1^{-1}
+P(\mathcal A_T^c\mid E_0)
\right\}\\
&\longrightarrow0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Let \(D_T=\widehat m_1-m(z_0)\).  The displayed target calculation and the
definition of \(\widehat\tau\) imply the exact decomposition
\[
\widehat\tau-\tau_n(z_0)=\Gamma-\frac14-D_T.
\]
By the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\left|
\mathbb E_P[(\widehat\tau-\tau_n(z_0))^2\mid E_0]
-\mathbb E_P[(\Gamma-1/4)^2\mid E_0]
\right|\\
&\quad\leq
2\{\mathbb E_P[(\Gamma-1/4)^2\mid E_0]\}^{1/2}
 \{\mathbb E_P[D_T^2\mid E_0]\}^{1/2}
+\mathbb E_P[D_T^2\mid E_0]
\longrightarrow0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(\Gamma\) is Bernoulli with success probability \(1/4\),
\[
\lim_{T\to\infty}
\mathbb E_P\!\left[(\widehat\tau-\tau_n(z_0))^2\mid E_0\right]
=\operatorname{Var}_P(\Gamma)
=\frac14\left(1-\frac14\right)=\frac3{16}.
\]

For this array, the four no-log components in
\texttt{def:rate-frontier} are
\[
R_{\mathrm{tr}}=n_1^{-1}=T^{-2},
\qquad
R_{\mathrm{sm}}=(Tn_1)^{-2/3}=T^{-2},
\]
\[
R_{\mathrm{sp}}=T^{-2},
\qquad
R_{\mathrm{don}}=N^{-1}=T^{-2}.
\]
Therefore \(R_\star=T^{-2}\), proving the rate assertion.

It remains to analyze \texttt{def:honest-interval}.  On \(\mathcal A_T\),
the successful local-constant weights are
\[
a_{1ti}=\frac{{\bf 1}\{t\in I_T\}}{n_1|I_T|},
\qquad
\sum_{t=1}^T|a_{1ti}|=\frac1{n_1},
\qquad
\sum_{t=1}^T\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}|a_{1ti}|=1.
\]
For each fixed \(\alpha\in(0,1/2)\), substitution into the two Hoeffding
radii yields
\[
R_{\mathrm{hist}}
=B\left\{\frac12\log\left(\frac2{\alpha_{\mathrm{hist}}}\right)
\frac1{n_1}\right\}^{1/2}=O(T^{-1}),
\]
\[
R_{\mathrm{evt}}
=B\left\{\frac12\log\left(\frac2{\alpha_{\mathrm{evt}}}\right)
\frac1{n_1}\right\}^{1/2}=O(T^{-1}).
\]
The support of \(K\), nonnegativity of the weights, and their unit total
mass give
\[
A_L\leq C_{0,1}L\underline h_T
=O\!\left(\frac{\log T}{T}\right).
\]
Here \(D=Sd=1\), so the exact donor calibration gives
\[
M_4(N)=\frac{16}{N}+3\left(1-\frac1N\right)\leq16,
\qquad
q_N=\{M_4(N)/\alpha_{\mathrm{don}}\}^{1/4}=O(1).
\]
Since \(c_\Sigma=C_\Sigma=1\) and \(\kappa=1\),
\[
\delta_N=\frac{q_N}{\sqrt N}=O(T^{-1}),
\qquad
A_{\mathrm{don}}=C_{\mathrm{mod}}\delta_N=O(T^{-1}).
\]
Consequently \(\delta_N\leq\delta_0\) for all sufficiently large \(T\).
On \(\mathcal A_T\), the selected Gram matrix is positive and every
required weight and radius is finite.  Hence, eventually, the bad-sample
event from \texttt{def:honest-interval} is contained in
\(\mathcal A_T^c\), while throughout \(\mathcal A_T\)
\[
H_\alpha
=R_{\mathrm{hist}}+R_{\mathrm{evt}}+A_L+A_{\mathrm{don}}
=O\!\left(\frac{\log T}{T}\right)=o(1).
\]
The implicit constant depends only on the fixed \(\alpha\) and fixed class
and procedural constants.  Thus, for all sufficiently large \(T\),
\(H_\alpha<1/8\) throughout \(\mathcal A_T\).

If the nonfallback interval contains \(\tau_n(z_0)\), then necessarily
\(|\widehat\tau-\tau_n(z_0)|\leq H_\alpha\).  But
\(|\Gamma-1/4|\geq1/4\) almost surely, and on
\(\{|D_T|<1/16\}\) the reverse triangle inequality gives
\[
|\widehat\tau-\tau_n(z_0)|
\geq\frac14-\frac1{16}=\frac3{16}>\frac18.
\]
Since fallback can eventually occur only in \(\mathcal A_T^c\),
\[
\{\tau_n(z_0)\in C_\alpha\}
\subseteq
\mathcal A_T^c\cup\{|D_T|\geq1/16\}.
\]
Therefore Markov's inequality, in the elementary form
\({\bf 1}\{|D_T|\geq1/16\}\leq256D_T^2\), yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
P\{\tau_n(z_0)\in C_\alpha\mid E_0\}
&\leq P(\mathcal A_T^c\mid E_0)
 +P(|D_T|\geq1/16\mid E_0)\\
&\leq P(\mathcal A_T^c\mid E_0)
 +256\,\mathbb E_P[D_T^2\mid E_0]
\longrightarrow0.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves the asserted coverage failure and completes the construction.

Fix a cohort \(s\) for which the normalized-shape fit succeeds.  Suppress the cohort subscript temporarily and put \(\mathsf L=L_s\), \(G=G_s\), and
\[
v_{ti}=w_{st}^{1/2}b_r(u_{st}).
\]
The kernel is nonnegative by \texttt{def:feasible-estimator}, so this square root is defined.  The definitions of \(G_s\), \(L_s\), and \(a_{sti}\) give
\[
G=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}v_{ti}v_{ti}^{\top},
\qquad
\mathsf L=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}w_{st},
\qquad
a_{sti}=w_{st}^{1/2}e_0^{\top}G^{-1}v_{ti}.
\tag{1}
\]
Success of the selector means both \(\mathsf L>0\) and
\[
G/\mathsf L\succeq c_G I_{q_r}.
\tag{2}
\]
In particular, \(G\) is invertible, as required in (1).  Applying Cauchy--Schwarz to (1), and then using the first identity in (1), yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}|a_{sti}|
&\le
\left\{\sum_{t,i}w_{st}\right\}^{1/2}
\left\{\sum_{t,i}
       (e_0^{\top}G^{-1}v_{ti})^2\right\}^{1/2}\\
&=\mathsf L^{1/2}
\{e_0^{\top}G^{-1}GG^{-1}e_0\}^{1/2}\\
&=\{\mathsf L e_0^{\top}G^{-1}e_0\}^{1/2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
\]
By (2), inversion reverses the Loewner order and hence
\[
G^{-1}\preceq(c_G\mathsf L)^{-1}I_{q_r}.
\tag{4}
\]
The monomial vector \(b_r\) contains the constant monomial and every nonconstant monomial vanishes at zero.  Thus the definition \(e_0=b_r(0)\) gives \(\|e_0\|_2=1\).  Combining (3) and (4) proves
\[
\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}|a_{sti}|
\le \{L_s e_0^{\top}G_s^{-1}e_0\}^{1/2}
\le c_G^{-1/2}.
\tag{5}
\]

For fixed \((s,t)\), the definitions of \(u_{st}\) and \(w_{st}\) do not involve \(i\).  Consequently
\[
G_s=n_s\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_{st}b_r(u_{st})b_r(u_{st})^{\top},
\]
and the definition of \(a_{sti}\) shows that \(a_{sti}\) is constant in \(i\).  Therefore (5) implies, for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n_s\}\),
\[
\sum_{t=1}^{T}|a_{sti}|
=\frac1{n_s}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i'=1}^{n_s}|a_{sti'}|
\le \frac{c_G^{-1/2}}{n_s}.
\tag{6}
\]
Using (6), the positivity of the cohort weights, and the definition of \(R_{\mathrm{tr}}\) in \texttt{def:rate-frontier}, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{s=1}^{S}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}
\left[\pi_s\sum_{t=1}^{T}|a_{sti}|\right]^2
&\le \sum_{s=1}^{S}n_s
\left(\frac{\pi_s c_G^{-1/2}}{n_s}\right)^2\\
&=c_G^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\frac{\pi_s^2}{n_s}
=c_G^{-1}R_{\mathrm{tr}}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}
\]

It remains to establish the Taylor-bias assertion.  If \(p(u)=c^{\top}b_r(u)\) is any polynomial of total degree at most \(r\), then the definitions of \(a_{sti}\) and \(G_s\) imply the exact reproduction identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}a_{sti}p(u_{st})
&=e_0^{\top}G_s^{-1}
  \sum_{t,i}w_{st}b_r(u_{st})b_r(u_{st})^{\top}c\\
&=e_0^{\top}G_s^{-1}G_sc
=e_0^{\top}c
=p(0).
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]
For each cohort, let \(P_s\) be the degree-\(r\) Taylor polynomial of \(m_s\) about \(\widetilde z_s\).  The function \(u\mapsto P_s(\widetilde z_s+h_su)\) has total degree at most \(r\), so (8) gives
\[
\sum_{t,i}a_{sti}P_s(X_{st})=P_s(\widetilde z_s)=m_s(\widetilde z_s).
\tag{9}
\]
Under \texttt{ass:holder-smoothness}, with \(r=\lceil\lambda\rceil-1\), the declared H\"older-ball Taylor remainder convention gives, for \(x,\widetilde z_s\in[0,1]^d\),
\[
|m_s(x)-P_s(x)|
\le C_{r,d}L\|x-\widetilde z_s\|_2^{\lambda}.
\tag{10}
\]
The cube projection in \texttt{def:feasible-estimator} ensures \(\widetilde z_s\in[0,1]^d\), while the support declaration gives \(X_{st}\in[0,1]^d\), so (10) applies to every summand.  From (9)--(10) and the triangle inequality,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\left|
\sum_{s=1}^{S}\pi_s
\left\{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}
a_{sti}m_s(X_{st})-m_s(\widetilde z_s)\right\}
\right|\\
&\qquad\le
C_{r,d}L\sum_{s=1}^{S}\pi_s
\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}|a_{sti}|
\|X_{st}-\widetilde z_s\|_2^{\lambda}
=A_L,
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]
where the last equality is the definition in \texttt{def:honest-interval}.  Equations (5), (6), (7), and (11) establish all claimed conclusions.  The argument used only the lower normalized-shape condition (2); at no point was an upper bound on \(L_s\) imposed.
